drainage.local_h: When sandy ground still holds water
local: White Oak's sandy soil drains well on its own, which is why the problems here tend to be specific. A downspout dumps right at the foundation. A flat spot has no fall to carry water off. A back corner stays soft long after the rest of the yard dries. We start by finding the cause, because the fix for a downspout is nothing like the fix for a low corner, and the first costs far less.

Sandy topsoil often sits over a firmer layer below it. Rain soaks the top, hits that layer and spreads sideways, and that is when water ends up where you did not expect it. We walk the property during or right after a rain when we can, so we can see where it comes from and where it sits. Digging goes faster in a dry stretch, so we plan the work around that.

The fix is picked to match the problem. A downspout extension or a solid-pipe reroute handles roof water. Regrading and swales move surface water. Pop-up emitters, catch basins and channel drains give it somewhere to go. A French drain with sock-wrapped pipe and #57 stone handles the rest. Every run gets a steady fall toward a real outlet, whether that is daylight, a lower part of the lot or an emitter.

We have seen the same principle on our own builds here. The raised boat and RV pad we finished in September 2026 was built with drainage fabric along the timber wall and a crushed concrete top, so rain moves through the pad instead of pooling on it. Pricing follows the work: small fixes run $450 to $1,000, a standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000, full systems run $3,000 to $4,500, and large combined jobs cost more.

faq.q: My White Oak yard is sandy, so why is one corner still soggy?
faq.a: Sandy topsoil often sits on a firmer layer. Once the top saturates, water spreads sideways and collects in low or flat spots. Downspouts emptying at the foundation make it worse. We find where the water collects and give it a path out.

faq.q: How much does drainage work cost?
faq.a: Small fixes like a downspout reroute or one low spot run $450 to $1,000. A standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000. Full systems run $3,000 to $4,500, and large or combined projects start at $4,500. Most projects land between $2,000 and $3,750.

faq.q: Do I need a French drain, or is something simpler enough?
faq.a: Often something simpler works. A downspout extension, a regrade or a swale and pop-up emitter solves many yards for far less. We only recommend a French drain when the water needs a buried path, and we explain why in the written estimate.

faq.q: Can you stop water from pooling against my foundation?
faq.a: Yes. We regrade so the ground slopes away from the house, extend or reroute downspouts into solid pipe and add a drain or emitter where the water needs to leave. We confirm the outlet before we start digging. Confirming the outlet first means we never bury a pipe that has nowhere to empty.

faq.q: When is the best time to call about drainage?
faq.a: Call while the problem is visible, during or right after a rain, so we can see it. We fix drainage year-round, and the work itself goes faster in a dry stretch. Getting it done before spring rains means one less season with a wet corner.

fertilization.local_h: On sandy ground, fertilizer goes fast and timing does the work
local: White Oak soil runs sandy. Water moves through it quickly, and the nutrients travel with it. One heavy feeding gets pulled below the roots by the first few storms, so the lawn gets a flush and then goes hungry. We lean on smaller, slower-release feedings timed to the season, so what goes down is still there when the grass can use it. That is the main difference between a White Oak plan and one written for clay.

The calendar is simple. The first feeding goes down around late April, once nights hold above 60 and the grass is fully awake. Then early July, early September and a potassium-heavy winterizer in October. Feed in March and most of it washes out with the next rain. Late nitrogen is the opposite mistake, especially on the St. Augustine under many White Oak oaks and pines, so our last real nitrogen goes down in early September.

Before we plan anything, we pull a soil sample. Years of pine needles and acidic rain push a lot of East Texas ground a little low on pH, and if the test says so, we add lime. The test also shows whether a thin patch is a nutrient problem at all. Under a closed canopy the trees take a share of the food and water, and some thin turf is really a shade problem that no bag of fertilizer will fix. We tell you which it is.

Compacted lawns get core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. Foot traffic and mower wheels pack the ground along paths and gates, even on sandy lots. We coordinate visits with your mowing schedule, and bigger lots outside the middle of town are priced from the lawn's size. We feed, aerate, test and advise. We do not apply weed or pest treatments. Ask us on the walkthrough whether your lawn is packed enough to need it.

faq.q: How many times a year should I feed my White Oak lawn?
faq.a: Most lawns do well on four visits: late April, early July, early September and an October winterizer. Sandy soil lets nutrients move through quickly, so smaller feedings spaced across the season hold up better than one big application in spring.

faq.q: What does fertilizing cost in White Oak?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. Seasonal programs are priced from your lawn size and the number of rounds it needs, and lime or aeration adds to the total. You see the plan and the price in writing before we apply anything.

faq.q: Should I feed the shaded St. Augustine under my trees?
faq.a: Yes, but carefully. Shaded turf uses less than a sunny lawn, and late nitrogen feeds large patch when October nights turn damp. We test the soil, hold the last nitrogen to early September and use potassium in the fall instead.

faq.q: Does the program include anything for weeds or insects?
faq.a: No. We do not apply weed or pest treatments. The program is soil testing, slow-release feeding, lime when the test calls for it, aeration and mowing advice. A well-fed lawn at the right height crowds out a lot on its own.

faq.q: When do you aerate lawns in White Oak?
faq.a: Compacted lawns get core aeration from late August through mid-September, with the feeding right behind it so the roots can use it. We look at the lawn on the walkthrough and tell you whether yours is packed enough to need it.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Building beds for a half day of sun
local: Many White Oak beds sit in dappled shade under mature oaks and pines, and that decides the plant list before anything else. On the walkthrough we count the hours of sun the bed gets, check how it drains after a rain, and ask what you want to see from the street and the porch. A bed that gets a half day of sun needs different plants than one baking at the front walk.

White Oak's sandy beds drain well, but they run low on nutrients and dry quickly. So the prep matters more than the plants. We cut the edge, pull weeds by the root, loosen the top of the soil and work in compost before a single plant goes in. Edging can be stone, steel or a natural cut. Compost gives the sand something to hold water with, and it feeds the roots through the first season.

For part shade, azaleas, hydrangeas, cast iron plant, holly ferns and caladiums do well here. Set in amended soil and mulched, they are not fighting the sand for water. In the sunnier beds we use lantana, salvia, plumbago and knockout roses, and wait until mid-May to plant heat lovers like vinca. A cool, wet spring rots them if they go in early. Shrubs and perennials do best in the fall.

Plants go in with real spacing so air moves through them, then mulch goes down at 1 to 1.5 inches and gets pulled back off the stems. We finish by walking you through watering, which is a deep soak instead of a daily sprinkle. If you want to see the bed drawn first, our $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars.

faq.q: Which plants work in a bed that only gets half a day of sun?
faq.a: Azaleas, hydrangeas, cast iron plant, holly ferns and caladiums all handle part shade in White Oak. We set them in amended soil with mulch on top. Sun plants like lantana and salvia are saved for the brighter beds, where they have what they need.

faq.q: How much does a new flower bed cost in White Oak?
faq.a: New beds are priced with our planting work, and most projects run $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. Bed size, plant count and size, edging and soil prep set the number, and you get it in writing.

faq.q: When should I plant my flower beds?
faq.a: Shrubs and perennials do best in fall, from September through November, while the soil is warm and the air is cooling. Heat lovers like vinca wait until mid-May or later. Seasonal color rotates with the weather so the bed has something blooming most of the year.

faq.q: Why do new beds die in their first summer?
faq.a: Usually it is the wrong plant for the light, heat lovers set out too early, or shallow watering. Sandy ground dries fast, so we amend with compost and tell you to water deep and less often. A good plant in the wrong spot is still a dead plant.

faq.q: Can I see a design before you plant?
faq.a: Yes. The $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering of the bed first. If you book the install within 90 days, the fee is credited toward the job. It is a good fit if you want to see the plant mix and layout before any ground is dug.

hardscaping.local_h: How we built a 475 square foot flagstone patio in White Oak
local: In August 2026 we finished about 475 square feet of Cherokee flagstone in a White Oak backyard, with chopped stone edging around a chopped stone fire pit. The yard falls away from the house, which is common on the larger lots around town, so the patio had to be built up to stay level. That job shows how we work here better than a list of materials does. Every patio we build starts the same way, with a plan for the slope.

The build starts with the ground. We dug out the area, filled it and compacted it with a plate compactor, then laid a sand setting bed for the flagstone. Where the yard drops, a chopped stone wall holds up one raised corner so the whole surface stays level. Flagstone was set and mortared around the fire pit, and the ground around it was backfilled and graded so water runs away from the stone.

Most patio failures in East Texas come from the dirt, not the stone. A lot of this area is sandy loam over red clay, and the clay swells after heavy spring rain and shrinks in a dry August. Stone laid on a thin bed of sand over that will settle and split. So we dig to the right depth, compact a crushed stone base and pitch the surface away from the house. Water getting under a patio is what undermines it.

Larger lots leave room for more than a single slab. Paver patios, flagstone paths, seating walls, outdoor kitchens and fire features are all part of what we build, with chopped stone borders to hold the edges. Most projects run $3,100 to $9,100, and the exact number comes in a written estimate after we walk the site. The $449 Hardscape Preview shows layouts first. hedge-trimming.local_h: Why hedges under White Oak's shade trees go leggy
local: Many White Oak lots are shaded by mature oaks and pines, and hedges under that canopy grow toward whatever light they can find. They stretch tall, thin out at the bottom and go bare at the base. A hedge sheared flat across the top makes it worse, because the top shades its own lower branches. We shape each one slightly narrower at the top than the base, so sun reaches the leaves down low.

Foundation shrubs on older White Oak homes are the other common job. Years of growth push them against the brick, across the windows and into the gutters. We cut them back off the walls, keep them clear of the glass and open them up so air moves through. Tarps go down first, and every clipping is raked up, blown out of the beds and hauled away, so you are not left with piles by the driveway.

Timing depends on the plant. June is the clean window for hollies and boxwoods. Azaleas and mophead hydrangeas get trimmed right after they bloom, because cutting them later removes next year's flowers. We skip hard shearing in late fall, since tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap. Most hedges want two to three trims between spring and fall, and we can set you up on that schedule. Cut at the wrong time, a shrub spends the season recovering instead of growing.

For a hedge that has gone far past shaping, a hard rejuvenation cut in late winter usually brings it back by summer. Some plants, old boxwoods in particular, return slowly, and a few are better replaced. We count the shrubs and tell you which is which at the walkthrough. A handful of foundation shrubs sits at the low end of the range, and long, tall hedges along a bigger lot's fence line run higher.

faq.q: Can a hedge that is bare at the bottom be saved?
faq.a: Usually. Most overgrown shrubs take a hard cut in late winter and fill back in by summer. Old boxwoods come back slowly, and a few plants are not worth the wait. We look at each one on the walkthrough and tell you honestly which to cut and which to replace.

faq.q: How much does hedge trimming cost in White Oak?
faq.a: Most jobs run $150 to $800. The number and size of the shrubs set the price, along with how overgrown they are, any formal shaping and how much we haul off. You get an itemized price in writing, usually within a day of the walkthrough.

faq.q: When is the best time to trim hedges?
faq.a: Spring through fall is the main season, with two to three trims for most hedges. June suits hollies and boxwoods. Flowering shrubs like azaleas wait until right after bloom. Late fall is the wrong time for hard shearing, because new growth gets burned by the first freeze.

faq.q: Do you haul away the clippings?
faq.a: Yes. Tarps go down before we cut, then every clipping is raked up, blown out of the beds and hauled off. We do not leave piles at the curb or bags for you to deal with. You get a clean bed and a clear drive when we finish.

faq.q: Will you cut off next year's flowers?
faq.a: Not if we can help it. Before cutting, we note which shrubs bloom on old wood, like azaleas and mophead hydrangeas, and time those trims for right after the flowers fade. That is part of the walkthrough, not a surprise afterward.

irrigation.local_h: Even coverage on ground that drinks fast
local: White Oak's sandy soil drinks water fast and dries out fast. That means coverage has to be even, or the lawn browns in strips by July. We space heads for full overlap so no stretch of grass depends on a single stream. Cycles are kept shorter so water soaks in instead of running off, and zones are split by slope as well as by sun, so a low corner is not flooded while the high side stays dry.

Many White Oak lots are half sun and half shade under mature oaks and pines, and one watering schedule cannot serve both. Sunny Bermuda and shaded St. Augustine need different amounts. So we lay out zones by sun, shade, turf and beds, and each gets its own run time. The controller is set up for the season, and we show you how to change it, so you are not watering in the rain.

Beds are the other mistake we see. Spray heads in a flower bed soak the leaves, the mulch and the side of the house and still leave the roots thirsty. We put beds and shrubs on drip, which puts the water at the roots, wastes almost none and keeps the foliage dry. On sandy ground that dries quickly, drip under a layer of mulch holds water where the plants can use it.

Installation covers more than pipe and heads. We pull the permit where the job requires one, put in a backflow prevention device on city water and add a rain or freeze sensor on new automatic systems. Every zone is run and adjusted for coverage, and the licensed irrigator checks the system before we call it done. Repairs cover heads, lines, valves and wiring. Larger lots mean more zones, which is why pricing comes after a walkthrough.

faq.q: Do you install sprinkler systems in White Oak?
faq.a: Yes, and we repair them too. The work is done under a Texas licensed irrigator, license LI0006657, who checks every system. White Oak is a short drive from Longview, and the walkthrough and the written quote are free. That is true whether it is a new install or a repair on an older system.

faq.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost?
faq.a: Every yard and water source is different, so we price irrigation after a free walkthrough. Size, the number of zones, turf heads versus bed drip, water pressure, slopes, trees and permit requirements all count. You get an itemized written quote, usually within a day.

faq.q: Do you repair systems you did not install?
faq.a: Yes. We fix heads, lines, valves and wiring on existing systems. We look at what the system is doing wrong, whether that is a dry strip, a head that sprays the street or a zone that will not turn on, then send a written quote before any work starts.

faq.q: Do I need a permit for a sprinkler system?
faq.a: Where the job requires one, we pull it. You do not have to chase paperwork. We also install a backflow prevention device on city water systems, which is part of doing the job correctly. Permit rules vary by job, which is why we ask about them at the walkthrough.

faq.q: Should my flower beds be on drip or spray?
faq.a: Drip, in almost every case. Spray in a bed wets the leaves and the siding and still misses the roots. Drip puts water where the plant uses it, and on White Oak's sandy ground a mulched bed on drip holds moisture far better.

landscaping.local_h: Reworking a White Oak yard around its trees
local: A lot of White Oak landscaping starts with a yard that has good bones and tired beds. The trees are in, the lot is established, and the beds have drifted over the years. Edges are lost, shrubs are overgrown, and nothing is planted for the light it gets now. We start by walking the property to see where the sun falls, where the shade sits and how the water moves after a rain.

The soil here is sandy. It drains well, but it runs low on nutrients and dries quickly, so we work compost into the beds before anything is planted. Trees and shrubs go in with the root flare at grade and native soil around them. Then each bed gets mulch or rock and a clean edge, so the lines hold up. We cut the bed lines, pull weeds by the root and loosen the compacted spots first.

Shade shapes the plant list. Under the oaks and pines we use shade-tolerant shrubs, ferns and ground covers, and mulch or stone where grass will not grow. Forcing sun plants under a closed canopy is a mistake we see a lot. In the open parts of the yard, lantana, salvia, plumbago, vinca and knockout roses handle the July heat. Azaleas and hydrangeas go only where they are sited right. Mulch or stone covers the bare ground under the trees.

On the bigger lots around White Oak, planting often pairs with something built. We finished a Cherokee flagstone patio around a fire pit here in August 2026, and walls or drainage can go in alongside the beds where the lot needs them. Fall, from September to about Thanksgiving, is the best planting window. If you want to see it first, a Design Preview gives you renderings before anything goes in the ground.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant in White Oak?
faq.a: Fall, from September to about Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm while the air cools, so trees and shrubs build roots for months before summer. Spring works for summer color, but woody plants set out in April spend their first summer trying to survive.

lawn-maintenance.local_h: Cutting a White Oak lawn that splits between shade and sun
local: A lot of White Oak yards sit under mature oaks and pines, and the canopy decides how the lawn grows. Where the trees close in, the grass is St. Augustine and it runs thin. Where the sun gets through, it is Bermuda and it fills in thick. One lot can hold both. We cut each patch at its own height instead of picking one setting for the whole yard, so the shaded side is not scalped and the sunny side is not left shaggy.

Height matters even more on sandy ground. White Oak soil drains fast and dries out fast, so a short cut leaves the roots exposed to July heat with nothing to hold moisture. Through summer we keep St. Augustine at three and a half to four inches and Bermuda at about two to two and a half. Taller blades shade the soil and push the roots deeper, which is the cheapest protection a lawn gets against a dry stretch.

Trunks, bed edges and fence lines are where mowing slows down. Mature trees mean a lot of string-trimming, and we trim around every trunk so the deck stays off the bark. Walks, drives and patios get blown clean at the end of each visit, and clippings go back into the turf. Lot size and tree cover are what move the price, so a shady quarter acre can cost more than an open one the same size.

Outside the middle of town the lots get bigger, and those are priced after a walkthrough instead of from the $65 starting rate. White Oak is right next to Longview, so adding a lawn here to a weekly route is easy to schedule. Most yards go weekly from late March through October, then every other week as growth slows. If we spot thin grass under the canopy or a patch that stays wet, we tell you early.

faq.q: Do you mow every week in White Oak?
faq.a: Yes. Weekly is our normal schedule from late March through October, and we drop to every other week as growth slows. White Oak is close to our Longview shop, so it fits easily into a route. You get a flat per-visit price in writing before the first mow.

faq.q: What does mowing cost for a bigger White Oak lot?
faq.a: Typical yards start at $65 per visit. Larger lots are priced after we walk them, because lot size, tree cover, trimming and gate access all change the time on site. Two lots the same size can price differently if one is wide open and the other is full of trunks and fence line.

faq.q: Why is the grass so thin under my oak trees?
faq.a: Shade is the usual reason. St. Augustine tolerates it better than Bermuda, but under a closed canopy even St. Augustine thins. We keep it mowed tall and tell you if a spot gets too little sun to hold turf, since that area may do better as a mulch bed than as lawn.

faq.q: Do you bag the clippings?
faq.a: No. Clippings are blown back into the turf, where they break down. Walks, drives and patios are blown clean when we finish. Leaves from the first part of fall get mulched back into the lawn with the mower, which saves a trip while the drop is still light.

faq.q: Can you also handle the leaves from my trees in the fall?
faq.a: Yes. Early leaves are mulched in on your regular mowing visits. When the oaks drop heavily, a full leaf cleanup is a separate service that we can quote alongside your mowing, so one crew knows the whole property. Heavy canopy can need a second pass in December, and we will say so on the walkthrough.

leaf-removal.local_h: Where the leaves end up on a White Oak property
local: Mature oaks and pines over many White Oak lots mean a heavy fall drop, and it does not stay on the lawn. Leaves blow to the fence, pack into back corners and fill the shrub beds. On the bigger properties nobody looks at those spots until spring. We walk the whole lot first, far corners included, so the flat price covers everything the trees dropped and not just the front yard.

The leaf vacuum trailer is the part most crews cannot match, and ours is the only one in the area. We blow leaves and pine straw out of the lawn, the beds and the rock beds onto the street or another paved surface, then vacuum them up. The trailer shreds them about 10 to 1, so a pile that would fill a yard goes away in one load. On a large lot, how far the leaves sit from the drive or street helps set the price.

Timing runs longer than most people expect. Most lots need a pass in the first half of November, another in mid-December and a last one before spring green-up, because oaks keep dropping into February. A big White Oak property under heavy canopy may need that December pass once the oaks finish. Before November, a light early drop is better mulched into the lawn by the mower than hauled off. The ground under the pines also collects needles, and we clear pine straw the same way.

Under the canopy the lawn is usually St. Augustine, and that is the grass that suffers from wet leaves. A thick mat over it while the soil is still in the 60s sets up large patch, and the dead circles show up in March. White Oak's sandy ground drains fast, but a packed leaf layer holds moisture right against the grass. We also re-edge bed lines the leaves buried and clear drives, walks and patios.

faq.q: How is leaf removal priced for a big White Oak lot?
faq.a: It is one flat price for the job, quoted in writing after a free walkthrough. Lot size, number of trees, how deep the leaves are, beds to clear and distance to the street all count. There are no bag fees and no hourly meter running while we work.

faq.q: Will I need a second visit in December?
faq.a: Often, yes. Oaks keep dropping into February, so many lots get a pass in mid-November, another in mid-December and a last one before spring. Heavy canopy over St. Augustine can need weekly clearing for three or four weeks. We lay out the passes when we walk the property.

faq.q: Can you get leaves out of my shrub beds and rock beds?
faq.a: Yes. We blow leaves and pine straw out of shrub beds and rock beds, then re-edge any bed lines the leaves covered. Drives, walks and patios are cleared in the same visit, so the property looks finished when we leave.

faq.q: What do you do with the leaves afterward?
faq.a: We vacuum them into the trailer, shred them about 10 to 1 and haul them away. Nothing is bagged, nothing is left at the curb and nothing gets mulched into your beds. The leaves leave with us. It all goes in one load, so the property is clear when the crew drives away.

faq.q: Do you clean gutters too?
faq.a: We clear exterior gutters as part of leaf work. If the oaks and pines drop onto your roof, mention it at the walkthrough and we will include the gutters in the written price so it is one visit. That way you get one price and one visit instead of two.

mulch-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes installs mulch in White Oak from our Longview base, just east on US 80. mulch-installation.local_h: What mulch does for sandy beds
local: On White Oak's sandy beds, mulch does the job the soil can't. Sand drains fast and holds little water, so a bed with no mulch dries out between rains, and the roots go with it. A layer on top keeps the moisture where the plants can reach it. That is why we pay attention to depth. Done right, the mulch holds water in the bed and still lets light rain through to the roots.

The depth we use is 1 to 1.5 inches over a prepped bed. Online calculators say three inches, but that number comes from snow country. Three inches here sheds light rain like a tarp, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover. We loosen the crusted top inch so water gets down, then top up to the right depth instead of piling new mulch on old. We never put fabric under it.

Mature oaks and pines mean a lot of beds around trunks. We pull mulch back off the trunk and off the foundation, so there is no volcano of mulch piled against the bark. Under the pines, pine straw is an option if you like the look, and hardwood, cypress, cedar and dyed black or brown are all available. Every bed gets its edges re-cut and weeds pulled by the root before the first shovelful goes down.

Late April through mid-May is the best window, right after the spring growth flush and before the heat. A second one runs from late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down ahead of the leaves. A top-dress over a layer that is still there costs a fraction of a full install. We measure the beds so you only pay for what they need, and use bagged mulch where access is tight.

faq.q: How much does mulch installation cost in White Oak?
faq.a: Most beds run $600 to $2,400. The square footage, the number of beds, the mulch type and how much edging and weed pulling is needed all matter. A fall top-dress over an existing layer usually costs a fraction of a full install.

faq.q: Why 1 to 1.5 inches and not three?
faq.a: Deeper mulch sheds light rain, holds moisture against stems and gives voles a place to hide. On sandy beds we would rather keep the layer thin and the soil underneath loosened, so water reaches the roots and the mulch stays a mulch.

faq.q: Can you use pine straw under my pines?
faq.a: Yes. Pine straw is available on request, and it looks natural under pines. We also install hardwood, cypress, cedar, and dyed black or brown mulch. Tell us what look you want and we will price the one you choose. Each one is priced from the bed measurements, not a flat guess.

faq.q: When should I refresh my mulch?
faq.a: Late April through mid-May is the main window, and late September through October suits a thin top-dress. We check what is left of the old layer before we order, so you do not pay for mulch you do not need.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under the mulch?
faq.a: No. Mulch is meant to break down into soil, and fabric stops that. We pull weeds by the root, loosen the soil and lay the mulch straight on the bed. Pulling weeds by the root first gives the bed a clean start.

retaining-walls.local_h: Two walls we built in White Oak, and what they show
local: In September 2026 we built a raised pad for a boat and RV beside a White Oak shed. The shed did not line up with the ground next to it, so we set a pressure-treated timber wall course by course along the pad line. Drainage fabric went down along the wall, and a track loader hauled in the fill. We compacted it with a plate compactor and raked crushed concrete across the top.

The month before, in August, a different White Oak wall solved a different problem. A backyard fell away from the house, so one corner of a flagstone patio sits up on a chopped stone wall. The wall is what keeps the patio level. Walls on bigger lots are often about making usable flat ground, not only holding back a slope, and both of these jobs started with that question. Both jobs came down to the same step: working out what the ground needed before choosing the material.

Water is what takes walls down. Clay swells when it is wet, and behind a wall that water builds pressure until the wall leans, bows and cracks. White Oak ground is sandy on top and drains well, but it can sit on firmer layers below. So every wall gets a gravel chimney and a perforated drain pipe at the bottom with a real outlet, and the first course is set dead level on a compacted crushed stone base.

Pick the material for the job. Timber suits a working pad like the boat and RV one, where it holds fill and gravel. Near the house or in the main yard, block or stone usually lasts longer and looks more finished. Taller walls get geogrid, and a wall tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan gets flagged at the walkthrough. Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in White Oak?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000. Height and length move the number most. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. Material, excavation, drainage and geogrid on taller walls add to it, all itemized in writing.

faq.q: Is a timber wall a good choice here?
faq.a: For the right job, yes. We used pressure-treated timber for the wall under a raised boat and RV pad, where it holds fill and gravel. Near the house or in the main yard, block or stone usually lasts longer and looks more finished.

faq.q: Can you build a raised pad for a boat or RV?
faq.a: Yes. Our White Oak pad used a timber retaining wall, drainage fabric, compacted dirt fill and crushed concrete raked level on top. The wall holds the fill, the fabric helps water pass through, and the compaction keeps the pad from settling.

faq.q: Does every wall need a drain behind it?
faq.a: Yes. We put a gravel chimney and a perforated drain pipe behind every wall, with an outlet that lets the water leave. Water pressure behind the wall is what makes walls lean and crack, and a drain is how you stop that.

faq.q: Can a leaning wall be fixed?
faq.a: Often, but it usually means a rebuild. A leaning wall means the base or the drainage failed. We take it down, compact a proper base, set it back up course by course and add drainage behind it. We tell you at the walkthrough if it can be saved.

sod-installation.lede: Bermuda for the open yard, St. Augustine under the trees, laid tight on a leveled base with a watering plan that fits White Oak's sandy ground.
sod-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes installs sod in White Oak from our base in Longview, just east on US 80. We strip old turf, level and amend the soil, then lay bermuda, St. Augustine or Zoysia with tight seams, starter fertilizer and a watering plan. Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
sod-installation.local_h: Laying sod on sandy ground under White Oak's trees
local: Sod takes quickly in White Oak's sandy ground, because the roots push into loose soil with little resistance. It also dries out just as quickly. That is why we hand you a written watering schedule with every install. Plan on a deep morning soak every day for the first two weeks, then taper to less frequent soaks once the roots knit. Skip it in July and a new lawn can brown out in a couple of weeks.

Sun picks the grass here, not the price. Many White Oak lots are half open and half under mature oaks and pines. In the open we usually lay Tif419 bermuda. Under the trees it is St. Augustine, in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on how much shade the spot needs. Bermuda in a shaded yard thins to dirt by August no matter how it is fed. Under about four hours of sun, a bed or mulch beats turf.

Prep is where a sod job is won. We strip the old turf and weeds to bare soil, regrade, then till two to three inches of compost or topsoil into the sand so it holds moisture better. The base is leveled and rolled before a single roll goes down. Seams are staggered and tight, with starter fertilizer underneath. Ground around a new patio or wall gets backfilled and graded too, and sod is a natural finish for it.

Bermuda goes down best from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September. St. Augustine needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy, so get it in by the end of September. Laid in November, it just sits there like a rug. Pricing is by the pallet from your measured square footage, and access for the pallets matters on larger lots. Patch repairs and plugs cost less than a full yard.

faq.q: What does sod installation cost in White Oak?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet from the square footage. A small patch repair costs less, and a full yard with heavy prep costs more. Grass type, old turf removal, grading and pallet access all move the number. You get it in writing first.

faq.q: Which grass should I choose for a shaded White Oak yard?
faq.a: St. Augustine, in most cases. Bermuda needs full sun and quits in shade. We walk the yard, note where sun actually falls in summer and recommend a grass, or a split, for each area. A spot under four hours of sun may be better as a mulch bed.

faq.q: How long do I water new sod?
faq.a: Every morning for the first two weeks, enough to keep the sod and the soil under it damp. After that we taper to deeper, less frequent soaks as the roots take hold. Sandy ground dries quickly, so a missed day in summer matters more here than on heavier soil.

faq.q: Can you replace just the dead patches?
faq.a: Yes. Patch repairs and plugs are part of the work, and they cost less than a full install. We first check why the spot died, since shade, compaction or a leak can kill new sod too. Matching the grass to the rest of the yard keeps the seams from showing.

faq.q: When is it too late to lay St. Augustine?
faq.a: Get it down by the end of September. It needs four to six weeks of growth before it goes dormant. Sod laid in November has little time to root, so we usually suggest waiting for spring. Spring, once the soil warms, is the better time to lay it.

tree-planting.title: Tree Planting in White Oak, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes

tree-planting.h1: Planting trees that survive White Oak's sandy summers

tree-planting.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes plants trees in White Oak, just west of our Longview base on US 80. We match the species to your soil, sun and space, set the root flare at grade, and leave a mulch ring and a written watering plan. The tree drives most of the cost, so we quote after a free walkthrough. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-planting.local_h: A new tree in sandy loam lives or dies on water
local: White Oak's sandy loam is easy to dig and drains well, so a new tree roots in without a fight. The catch is the same thing that makes it easy. The ground holds very little water, and a young tree has almost no reach. For the first two summers, how you water decides whether it lives. We dig a wide, shallow hole, cut any circling roots, backfill with the native soil and leave you a plan you can follow.

Fall is the best window, from September until around Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools, so a tree planted in October gets close to six months of root growth before summer. A tree planted in April gets about eight weeks. We plant year-round, but a spring tree asks for a lot more water to get through its first August, and on sandy ground that gap shows fast.

Here is what a new tree is really drinking from. A container tree comes in a ball of light potting mix, and the yard around it is a different texture. Until roots grow out into native soil, the tree is living in a buried pot that dries in a day or two in July. Soak the ball with a trickling hose for about twenty minutes, twice a week for six weeks in fall, then weekly through November.

Where the tree goes matters as much as how. On the bigger lots around White Oak there is room for a shade tree well away from the house and the power lines, while an established in-town lot may only have one open spot among the old oaks. We read the sun, the drainage and the mature size before we pick a species. We would usually rather plant a smaller tree that roots in fast, and on bigger installs we check back around the 30-day mark.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a tree in White Oak?
faq.a: September through about Thanksgiving. Soil stays warm while the air cools, so the roots keep growing for months before summer heat. Spring planting works too, but the tree has far less time to establish and needs steady watering through its first summer.

faq.q: How much does tree planting cost?
faq.a: We do not publish a flat price, because the tree itself drives most of the cost. Species, size at planting, number of trees, site access and staking all count. We walk the spot, recommend a tree and send a written quote that includes the aftercare plan.

faq.q: How often do I water a newly planted tree?
faq.a: For a fall tree, soak the root ball twice a week for the first six weeks, weekly through November, then every ten to fourteen days in a dry winter. Water the day before a hard freeze. Sandy ground drains fast, so do not skip the schedule because the surface looks damp.

faq.q: Should I buy a bigger tree to get shade faster?
faq.a: Usually not. A smaller tree roots in faster and often catches up to a larger one within a few seasons. We pick healthy stock from regional growers and tell you which size makes sense for your spot. Bigger trees also cost more and take more water to get through the first summer.

faq.q: Do you stake new trees?
faq.a: Only when the site calls for it, such as a windy, exposed spot. Most trees on a sheltered lot do better without stakes. We build a watering basin and a mulch ring pulled back off the trunk on every tree we plant.

tree-shrub-care.title: Tree & Shrub Pruning in White Oak, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes
tree-shrub-care.meta: Tree and shrub pruning, shaping and small tree removal in White Oak, TX for established lots. Quoted after a free walkthrough, with full haul off.

tree-shrub-care.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes handles tree and shrub care in White Oak, just west of our Longview base on US 80. We prune by species and season, thin crepe myrtles instead of topping them, remove small trees and shrubs, and haul off every cut. Because no two yards have the same plants, we quote after a free walkthrough. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-shrub-care.local_h: Pruning an established White Oak lot, one species at a time
local: On older White Oak lots the work is usually catch-up. Shrubs have outgrown the beds they were planted in. Crepe myrtles have been cut the wrong way for years. A low limb drags across a shed roof, or a branch shades out the grass below it. On the walkthrough we identify each tree and shrub, flag what needs work and tell you what to leave alone, then put it all in a written quote.

Mature oaks are common here, and oaks get their own calendar. Oak wilt spreads partly through beetles drawn to fresh pruning cuts, and they are most active in spring and early summer. So we prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer. When a storm breaks an oak limb, we cut it clean and seal the wound right away. We also clear dead lower limbs off shade trees and haul out the storm debris.

Crepe myrtles and knockout roses get cut in February, while they are dormant. Azaleas are done right after bloom, and hollies and boxwoods in early summer. Topped crepe myrtles take longer. Topping makes the tree regrow on weaker wood, and recovery runs two or three winters, so we plan it out and come back each dormant season. We thin instead of topping, and we make cuts at the branch collar.

Know where we stop. We remove small trees and shrubs that have run their course. A large tree close to a house or power lines is a job for a tree service with the right equipment, and we say so up front rather than take it on. Seasonal feeding for trees and shrubs and a mulch refresh around the base are available too. Everything we cut leaves with us. Tell us what bothers you about a tree and we will say whether it is ours to fix.

faq.q: Can you take down a big oak next to my house?
faq.a: No. We remove small trees and shrubs. Large trees near a house or power lines need a tree service with the right equipment, and we will tell you that at the walkthrough. We do prune, shape and clean up everything we can safely reach.

faq.q: When should crepe myrtles be pruned in White Oak?
faq.a: February, while they are dormant and before the buds break. We thin them to the strongest branches rather than topping them. Chopping a crepe myrtle back to stubs gives you a tight mop of weak growth, not a smaller tree.

faq.q: Can a crepe myrtle that was topped years ago be fixed?
faq.a: Partly. Recovery takes two or three winters. We remove the weak shoots, rebuild the structure a little each dormant season and come back to finish it. If the tree is simply too big for the spot, a smaller variety is the real fix.

faq.q: Is it okay to prune my oak in spring?
faq.a: We avoid it. Oak wilt spreads through beetles that are drawn to fresh cuts in spring and early summer. We prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer, and we seal a storm-broken limb right after we cut it.

faq.q: How is tree and shrub care priced?
faq.a: We quote after a free walkthrough, because the number of plants, their size and condition, any small removals and the debris to haul all change the job. You get an itemized written quote, usually within a day. Small removals and storm cleanup show up as their own lines.
